label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
# The house in Glenmore

I have some news, and I'd sooner tell it to all of you at once, here, properly, than have it go round the family in bits and pieces on the phone. So I'll start with the part that matters most and the date, so nobody hears it from anyone else again.

I've sold the house in Glenmore. The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November and it closes on the 15th of January.

I know some of you had heard that before I got to tell you, and I'll come to that further down, because it's the part I'm least proud of. First I want to tell you why, and what's being kept, because you have a right to both.

## The house

For those of you who know it only from photographs, it's the old Mulkerrin place outside Oughterard, built in 1931 by Tom's grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. Tom grew up in it. It was never a grand house. It was a solid one, built by a man who meant it to last, and it did.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I've been driving out there every fortnight. It's forty minutes each way. I air the rooms, run the taps, check the pipes, look at the ceilings for any sign of new damp, and then I drive home again. I did it without complaint for a long time and I won't pretend it was a burden at the start. It gave me somewhere to go and something to do, and I think I needed that. But it has been going on for nearly two years now, and I have come to see that I can't keep it up.

## The practical reasons

I'll give you the sensible reasons first, because they're real, and then the one I find harder to say.

In September I had the roof surveyed by Ó Flaithearta's. The slates need doing and so does the back chimney, and the quote came to €38,000. On top of that there's damp in the back bedroom that has been creeping for a while, and the septic tank needs replacing. That last one has to be done to sell the house to anyone at all, so it wasn't something I could dodge by being clever about it.

I sat at the kitchen table with that quote for a good while. It's a lot of money to put into a house that nobody lives in, and I'd be putting it in at seventy-one. I'd also be taking on the workmen, the scaffolding, the weeks of it, and then the same again for the damp. And at the end of all that, I'd still be driving out every fortnight to check the pipes.

## The harder reason

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door. There was frost on it, and I went down hard. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get myself up. Nobody was passing, nobody knew where I was, and my phone was in the car.

I got up in the end, drove home, and told nobody. Not one of you. I'm telling you now, and I'm sorry if it's a shock to read it here. I didn't want anyone worrying, and I think I also didn't want to hear myself say it out loud, because if I said it I'd have to do something about it.

Since then I've been afraid of being out at that house on my own. I go in with my heart going a bit faster than it should, and I watch where I put my feet, and I don't stay as long. That's no way to look after a house, and it's no way to treat a house you love either. I can't go on maintaining it. That's the plain truth of it. The roof and the septic tank are the reasons I could put in a letter to a solicitor, but the fall is the one that decided me.

## Who's buying it

The buyers are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he knows the area and knows what he's taking on. They have two small children, and they want to live in the house. It won't be a holiday let and it won't be left sitting empty for eleven months of the year.

I should say that they weren't the only offer. In the summer a crowd from Dublin offered more than the Joyces have agreed to pay. The Joyces' price was fair, and I took the lower offer on purpose. I'd rather the house went to people who'll light the fire in it every evening than to people who'll want it for a few weekends in August.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. He said it more than once, usually when somebody had gone round the place with a dust cloth and told the children not to touch things. I think of that every time I'm out there with the windows open, listening to how quiet it is. Two small children will fix that quickly.

## What's being kept

I don't want anyone thinking the house is being emptied into a skip, so here's what is staying in the family.

The dresser is going to Úna's. Pádraig's fiddle is staying with us, and so are the photographs, all of them. The Sacred Heart lamp is coming too, and so is the sign from the gate.

The Joyces have also said, without my asking, that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I'm glad of that. They'll be the ones living there and I'd understand if they wanted their privacy, but they've offered, and I believe they mean it. So the fields aren't shut to us, and neither is the lake.

## What the house was, and what it wasn't

I've been thinking a lot about the things I'd never be able to take out of that house, and I keep coming back to the same ones.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house, in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. I said yes mostly because I wanted to get in out of the wet. That isn't quite true, but it's the version Tom always told, and I never contradicted him.

And the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan wouldn't come out of the water. We called and called, and he stayed in until his lips were blue, and even then he went on arguing that he wasn't cold. I can see it as clearly as if it were last summer.

Those memories aren't in the slates or the chimney or the walls of the back bedroom. They're in me, and they're in you. They'll be exactly as true on the 16th of January as they are today. It has taken me the best part of two years to understand that, and I'm not sure I'd have got there any sooner if I'd been given more time. I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I couldn't have said that in the first winter, and I can say it now.

## How you found out

Now to the part I'd rather skip, which is how some of you heard.

Declan heard it from his cousin Gráinne, on a WhatsApp, and not from me. That's my fault and nobody else's. I'd told a few people, I'd meant to ring the rest, I kept putting it off because I knew it would be a hard call to make, and the news got ahead of me. I should have rung every one of you myself before a word of it went anywhere. I didn't, and I'm sorry for that. I'm sorry for how you found out, and I'm especially sorry that Declan found out the way he did.

He rang me at two in the morning his time. He said I was selling Dad. I said things back to him that I shouldn't have, and I won't repeat them here, because they were said in a temper and I'd take them back if I could. For thirty years I taught small children to own up when they'd said something unkind, and then I went and did it myself on the phone. I'd like to think I'd have been gentler if I hadn't been caught off guard, but that's an excuse, and I'd not have accepted it from a seven-year-old.

I also regret not consulting Declan before the decision was made. He should have been asked, and I should have asked him. What I wasn't willing to do was wait until his visit in the summer, and I want to be honest about why. The roof wasn't going to wait, and neither was I. There was a buyer I trusted, and I'd been frightened at that back door for the best part of a year. I couldn't put it off for another winter of driving out there on my own. So I made the decision, and I stand by it. I'm sorry for the way it was done, but I'm not sorry that I did it, and I'd be lying if I told you otherwise.

## To Declan

Declan, I know you read these, so I'll say this directly to you. I'm not angry. I was hurt, and I think you were too, and two people who are hurt at two in the morning don't say their best things. That's all it was.

You have every right to grieve that house. It was your father's home and yours. You're allowed to be sad about it, and you're allowed to be sad with me or without me. I'm not asking you to agree with what I've done. I only want you to know that the door is open, and that it stays open. Ring me any time. I mean that, and I'll pick up.

## Sunday the 13th of December

Before the house is cleared, I'd like us to have a day out there together, one last family day while it's still ours.

It's Sunday the 13th of December. Anyone who can come is very welcome, and I'll do soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the haggard will be wet, as it always is, and if you want to see the lake you'll need them.

I know Boston and Perth and Leeds are a long way to come for a bowl of soup, and I don't expect anyone to cross the world for it. If you can't be there, I'd love to hear a memory of the house in the comments below. Something small is fine. Pádraig's fiddle is going to hear a few stories.

And if you can come, please come. It would mean a great deal to me to have the house full one more time, with people in every room and muck on the floor, the way Tom liked it.

The sale closes on the 15th of January. I wanted you all to hear it from me, and I'm only sorry that some of you didn't.

[Your name]

---

A few things to check before you post it:

- **Sign-off.** I left a placeholder, since I don't know what the cousins call you.
- **Time of day.** You didn't give a start time for the 13th, so I wrote "anyone who can come" without one. You may want to add it.
- **Úna's relation to you.** I never say what she is, so adjust if you'd like to.
- **Things people might want.** Some of the family may ask whether they can take something from the house before it's cleared. You haven't said either way, so I left it out, but you might want a line on it.
